usage: Let me treat you (to a meal)
Said when you want to pay and host; warmer and more formal than 제가 살게요, which is just 'I'll pay.'
Passive 대접받다 = to be treated/hosted; a natural thank-you after visiting someone's home.
treating someone as a guest / hospitality
The bare noun 대접 + 하다; 손님 대접을 하다 means to receive someone with proper hospitality.
to host lavishly / wine and dine
융숭하게 = generously, with great care; a set adverb that intensifies the hosting.
examples: 오늘은 제가 대접할게요.
Today it's my treat.
The everyday host line at a restaurant when you insist on paying; -ㄹ게요 signals a warm offer.
집에 초대해서 한정식으로 대접했어요.
I invited them over and hosted them with a Korean set meal.
한정식으로 대접하다 = host with N; the 으로 marks what you served. Implies real hosting effort.
손님을 이렇게 대접하면 안 되죠.
You shouldn't treat a customer like this.
Shows the wider sense: 대접하다 also = how you treat people (service quality), not only feeding them.
nuance: 대접하다 is Sino-Korean (待接, 待 'receive/wait on' + 接 'meet/connect'), so its core is 'receiving someone and attending to them' — usually by serving food, but also by how respectfully you treat a person. The near-synonym is 사다 ('buy a meal'): 사다 just means you pay, while 대접하다 adds hosting, effort, and respect, typically toward an elder, a guest, or a client. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (대접해요, 대접했어요), and in the negative the 하다 splits off (대접 안 해요). The very common passive 대접받다 ('be treated/hosted') is as frequent as the active. English speakers wrongly stretch 대접하다 to tiny favors ('I'll get this coffee') — for casual treats say 제가 살게요 and reserve 대접하다 for proper hosting.

Saying 대접해요 to mean only 'pay' — it bundles serving/hosting too, so 'I'll pay but you cook' doesn't fit 대접하다; use 계산하다/내다 for the bill alone.
Forgetting the passive: after being hosted, the natural thank-you is 잘 대접받았어요, not the active 잘 대접했어요 (which would mean you hosted them).

english: to help out / to lend a hand
usage: Offering to pitch in on a hands-on task like carrying, cooking, or cleaning up.
Can you help out a bit?
Casual request to a friend or family member to lend a hand with a chore in progress.
to help with the work / pitch in
일손 = a helping hand/labor; 일손을 거들다 is a set phrase for chipping in on busy work.
to chime in / back someone up in talk
The figurative sense: adding supportive words to a conversation already underway.
examples: 엄마 설거지 좀 거들어.
Help your mom with the dishes a bit.
거들다 = chip in on a task someone is already doing, rather than doing the whole thing for them.
이삿짐 옮기는 거 거들어 줄게요.
I'll help out moving the boxes.
거들어 주다 = lend a hand for someone's benefit; very natural for moving day among friends.
옆에서 말로만 거들지 말고 직접 좀 해.
Stop just chiming in from the side and actually do it yourself.
Here 거들다 = add words/back someone up; 말로만 거들다 = 'help only with your mouth.'
nuance: 거들다 means to pitch in on a task that is already in progress — you are a secondary helper, not the main doer. The dividing line vs 돕다 (the general 'help') matters: 돕다 can be the primary act of helping or even rescuing, while 거들다 is lighter, side-by-side assistance ('lend a hand'), so you'd never 거들다 a drowning person. It also has a figurative sense, 말을 거들다 ('chime in, back someone up' in conversation). Crucially it is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 거듭니다 (never 거들습니다), but the ㄹ stays everywhere else (거들어요, 거들 거예요, 거들지 마세요). English speakers also tend to use it for serious help, where 돕다 is correct.

Dropping the ㄹ where it should stay — the present is 거들어요, not 거어요; the ㄹ only disappears before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ.

usage: Asking someone to offer a seat — often to an elderly or pregnant passenger on the subway.
I'll give in / let it go this time
Conceding in a disagreement to keep the peace; very common in relationships and among friends.
to each take a step back / meet halfway
한 발씩 = one step each; a set idiom for mutual compromise so neither side wins fully.
Noun + nothing; a road-etiquette term for letting others merge and yielding right of way.
examples: 이번엔 내가 양보할게.
I'll give in this time.
Everyday concession to keep harmony; 양보하다 here = back down, not literally hand something over.
지하철에서 할머니께 자리를 양보했어요.
I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
Classic 양보 scene; 께 is the honorific 'to' for the older person, raising the recipient.
서로 한 발씩 양보하면 좋잖아.
It's nice if we each give a little, right?
한 발씩 양보하다 = 'each take a step back / compromise,' a fixed expression for meeting halfway.
nuance: 양보하다 is Sino-Korean (讓步, 讓 'yield/cede' + 步 'step' — literally 'yield a step'), and it covers both physical yielding (a seat, the right of way) and figurative conceding (backing down in an argument, letting someone have their way). The key contrast is with 포기하다 ('give up entirely'): 양보하다 means you give way to another person out of courtesy and could have kept it, whereas 포기하다 means you abandon a goal altogether. Culturally the nuance is positive — yielding is considerate, not weak — which is why you see the bare noun 양보 on subway signs and in driving etiquette (양보 운전). As a 하다-verb it's regular (양보해요), splitting in the negative (양보 안 해요). Don't confuse it with 포기하다 or with simply losing.

Marking the recipient with 을/를: it's 할머니께 자리를 양보하다 — the seat takes 을/를 and the person takes 께/한테, not the other way around.
Reading 양보 as defeat — saying 내가 양보할게 is a gracious 'I'll let it go,' not an admission that you lost; the tone is courteous, not bitter.

usage: You don't have to come see me off
Politely telling a host not to walk you out; 나오다 = come out (to the door/gate).
I saw them off all the way to the airport
까지 marks how far you went; going far shows you cared about the farewell.
to go out to see someone off
배웅 + 나가다; the act of stepping out to the door or gate to send someone off.
배웅 + 인사 (greeting); the goodbye words and gestures exchanged as someone leaves.
examples: 다음에 또 와, 하면서 배웅해 줬어요.
They saw me off saying 'come again next time.'
A natural parting scene after visiting someone's home; -아/어 주다 frames it as kindness done for you.
친구가 떠나는 게 아쉬워서 역까지 배웅했어.
I was sad my friend was leaving, so I saw them off at the station.
역까지 배웅하다 = accompany a departing person as far as the station; 까지 marks the distance.
할머니가 문 앞까지 나와서 배웅해 주셨어요.
Grandma came out to the door to see me off.
Common Korean courtesy — older hosts walk guests out; -아/어 주시다 honors the kindness done for you.
nuance: 배웅하다 means to accompany someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, the station, or the airport — and it is the exact counterpart of 마중하다 ('to go meet someone arriving'). Keep that pair straight: 배웅 is for departures, 마중 is for arrivals, and learners constantly swap them. It differs from a plain goodbye (인사하다/잘 가) because it implies physically going part of the way with the person, which signals warmth and respect; declining a host's offer ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself a polite gesture. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (배웅해요, 배웅했어요) and splits in the negative (배웅 안 해요); the noun 배웅 also stands alone in 배웅 나가다 and 배웅 인사.

mistakes: Swapping 배웅하다 (see off / departure) with 마중하다 (meet / arrival) — they are opposites; you 배웅하다 someone leaving and 마중하다 someone arriving.
Treating 배웅하다 as a mere verbal goodbye — it implies actually walking the person out or going part of the way, so just waving and saying 잘 가 is not yet 배웅.
Forcing an English 'see off' object pattern — it's 친구를 배웅하다 (person takes 을/를); don't add an extra 'off' particle or say 친구에게 배웅하다.

usage: to welcome / on the occasion of the new year
A very common set phrase opening greetings, sales, and announcements; N을/를 맞이해서 = 'to mark N.'
Said about a host, family, or company that received you kindly; 따뜻하게 = warmly.
The people sense; pairs with arriving guests or customers being welcomed in.
to greet a holiday / as the holiday comes
The occasion sense; 명절(설·추석) 맞이 is a fixed festive collocation.
examples: 사장님이 직접 나와서 손님을 맞이했어요.
The owner came out personally to welcome the guests.
맞이하다 = receive/greet an arrival; warmer and more formal than a plain 만나다 ('meet').
새해를 맞이해서 가족끼리 떡국을 먹었어요.
To welcome the new year, my family ate rice-cake soup together.
N을/를 맞이해서 = 'on the occasion of / to welcome N'; the fixed pattern for holidays and events.
곧 30대를 맞이하는 기분이 묘해요.
It feels strange to be about to enter my 30s.
맞이하다 also marks reaching a new life stage; here it frames turning thirty as something you 'greet.'
nuance: 맞이하다 means to welcome or receive, and it works in two registers: greeting an arriving person (손님을 맞이하다) and greeting an occasion or new phase (새해를/명절을/30대를 맞이하다). For people it overlaps with 마중하다 ('go out to meet an arrival') but sounds warmer and more formal and doesn't require going out to fetch them; against 만나다 ('meet'), 만나다 is a neutral two-way encounter, while 맞이하다 frames you as the host receiving someone. The everyday spoken cousin is 맞다 ('손님 맞을 준비'), but 맞이하다 is the clearer dictionary form. It is a regular 하다-verb (맞이해요, 맞이했어요), splitting in the negative (맞이 안 해요). Watch the look-alike 맞추다 ('fit/match/set'), an entirely different verb.

mistakes: Confusing 맞이하다 (welcome/receive) with 맞추다 (fit/match/set) — they look similar but are unrelated verbs; 시간을 맞추다 ≠ 손님을 맞이하다.
Using 만나다 where 맞이하다 is meant — 만나다 is a neutral mutual 'meet,' but greeting an arriving guest as the host is 맞이하다.
Misattaching the occasion phrase — it's 새해를 맞이해서 (object 을/를), not 새해에 맞이해서; the event you welcome takes 을/를.

english: to break / to violate (a rule or promise)
usage: The single most common collocation; failing to keep your word to someone.
규칙/법/신호 등을 어기다 = to violate rules, laws, or signals.
법(法) 'law' + 어기다; the standard phrasing for legal violation.
to run / ignore a traffic signal
신호 = traffic light/signal; a practical safety collocation for crossing on red.
examples: 또 약속을 어겨서 친구가 화났어.
I broke my promise again, so my friend got angry.
약속을 어기다 is the go-to phrase for letting someone down by not keeping your word.
신호를 어기고 건너면 위험해요.
It's dangerous to cross against the signal.
신호를 어기다 = ignore/run a traffic signal; -고 chains it to the next action (crossing).
회사 규정을 어기면 불이익이 있어요.
If you break company rules, there are penalties.
규정을 어기다 = violate regulations; 불이익 = disadvantage/penalty, a common workplace word.
nuance: 어기다 is the standard verb for breaking something intangible that you are bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), a signal (신호), or an appointment. Its direct antonym is 지키다 ('keep/abide by'), and the cleanest way to learn it is as that opposite: you either 지키다 or 어기다 a 약속. The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that English 'break' covers both rules and physical objects, but 어기다 only works for the intangible — a broken cup or phone is 깨다/부수다/고장 내다, never 어기다. It is a regular verb (어겨요, 어겼어요, 어기지 마세요), and in practice the natural negative command is 어기지 마세요 rather than 지키지 마세요.

Translating 'I broke up with my friend' as 친구를 어기다 — that's nonsense in Korean; 어기다 never takes a person as object. Use 헤어지다/절교하다 for relationships.

english: to keep / to protect / to abide by
usage: Be sure to keep your promise
The opposite of 약속을 어기다; pressing someone to follow through on their word.
거리를/순서를/규칙을 지키다 = keep distance/order/rules; a very common public request.
Everyday trust vocabulary; 비밀 지켜 줄 수 있어? = 'can you keep this secret?'
The protect/guard sense; pairs with 가족·집·사람 too (지켜 주다 = protect for someone).
examples: 나는 약속은 무조건 지켜.
I always keep my promises no matter what.
약속을 지키다 = keep one's word; 무조건 = unconditionally/no matter what, stressing reliability.
줄 설 때 순서 좀 지켜 주세요.
Please follow the order when lining up.
순서를 지키다 = wait your turn / keep the order; -아/어 주세요 makes it a polite request.
비밀 꼭 지켜 줄 수 있어?
Can you definitely keep this a secret?
비밀을 지키다 = keep a secret; -아/어 주다 frames it as a favor done for the speaker.
nuance: 지키다 is a high-frequency verb covering three linked senses: keep (a promise, a secret, a time/appointment), abide by (rules, order, manners, distance), and protect/guard (a person, a home, a country). For promises and rules it is the direct antonym of 어기다, so learning the pair together fixes both. Against 보호하다 ('protect' — more formal/abstract, e.g. 환경을 보호하다), 지키다 is the everyday, hands-on 'guard/defend' and also carries the 'keep/abide by' meanings that 보호하다 lacks. The English idiom 'keep a promise' transfers, but 'keep' in the sense of physically retaining something is 가지다/두다, not 지키다. It is a regular verb (지켜요, 지켰어요); note that the literal negative 지키지 마세요 is rarely used — to tell someone not to break a rule you say 어기지 마세요.

Overextending 'keep' — 'keep the receipt / keep it in your bag' is 가지고 있다/두다, not 지키다; 지키다 is keep-a-promise/guard, not keep-an-object.
Using 지키지 마세요 to warn against rule-breaking — that literally means 'don't keep it'; the natural phrase is 어기지 마세요 ('don't break it').

english: to show kindness / to be generous
usage: to show kindness / do someone a great favor
은혜/호의/친절을 베풀다 = bestow a kindness; slightly formal and heartfelt in tone.
Treat us / be generous and pay
Playful way to ask someone to treat the group, e.g. when they got good news or a raise.
인심 = warm-hearted generosity; describes giving freely, often extra food or help.
The 'lay on / put on (an event)' sense; somewhat literary, used for feasts and banquets.
examples: 사장님이 직원들한테 항상 잘 베풀어요.
The boss is always generous to the employees.
잘 베풀다 = be generous/giving; 한테 marks the people who receive the kindness.
어려울 때 도움을 베풀어 주셔서 감사해요.
Thank you for extending help when times were hard.
도움을 베풀다 = extend help; more elevated and grateful-sounding than plain 도와주다.
남한테 베푼 만큼 돌아온다고 하잖아.
They say what you give to others comes back to you.
A common saying about generosity (karma-like); 만큼 = 'as much as,' linking giving and return.
nuance: 베풀다 means to give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors, even a feast — usually from a position of being able to give, which is why it suits a boss, an elder, or a benefactor. It is warmer and more elevated than the plain 주다 ('give'), and it pairs with abstract nouns (은혜, 호의, 친절, 인심, 도움) rather than concrete objects: 선물을 베풀다 sounds odd, while 친절을 베풀다 is natural. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 베풉니다 (never 베풀습니다), but the ㄹ stays elsewhere (베풀어요, 베풀 거예요, 베풀지 마세요). The biggest English-speaker trap is reaching for it as a generic 'give'; keep it for bestowing intangible kindness.

structuredNuance.t: To give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors, even a feast — usually from a position of being able to give, which is why it suits a boss, an elder, or a benefactor.
It is warmer and more elevated than the plain 주다 ('give'), and it pairs with abstract nouns (은혜, 호의, 친절, 인심, 도움) rather than concrete objects: 선물을 베풀다 sounds odd, while 친절을 베풀다 is natural.
It is a ㄹ-irregular verb — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 베풉니다 (never 베풀습니다), but the ㄹ stays elsewhere (베풀어요, 베풀 거예요, 베풀지 마세요).
The biggest English-speaker trap is reaching for it as a generic 'give'; keep it for bestowing intangible kindness.

mistakes: Writing the formal form as 베풀습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving 베풉니다.
Using 베풀다 with concrete gifts (선물을 베풀다 sounds unnatural) — pair it with abstract kindness like 친절/호의/도움; for physical objects use 주다/선물하다.
Treating it as neutral everyday 'give' — 베풀다 implies giving generously from a higher/able position; between equals for small things, plain 주다 or 도와주다 fits better.

usage: Dividing food or a bill evenly with someone; 반씩 = half each.
Let's have a chat / talk things over
이야기를 나누다 = to converse; warmer and more mutual than a plain 말하다.
나누다 + 먹다, an extremely common combo for splitting and eating something with others.
The emotional-sharing sense; opening up about troubles so they feel lighter.
examples: 피자 한 판 시켜서 친구랑 나눠 먹었어요.
I ordered a pizza and shared it with a friend.
나눠 먹다 = share food; 친구랑 marks the partner you split and ate it with.
계산은 셋이서 똑같이 나눴어요.
We split the bill evenly among the three of us.
Splitting the check (n빵/더치페이); 나누다 is the verb for dividing the cost, 똑같이 = evenly.
그 친구랑 고민을 나누면 마음이 편해져요.
Sharing my worries with that friend puts me at ease.
고민을 나누다 = share one's worries; shows 나누다 extends to feelings and talk, not just things.
nuance: 나누다 holds two linked ideas: to divide (split a bill, cut into portions, partition) and to share (food, feelings, conversation). The 'share' sense is the warm heart of the word and surfaces in set combos like 나눠 먹다 (share food) and 이야기를/고민을 나누다 (share talk or worries) — sharing *with* someone, not a cold mathematical split. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the digital sense of 'share': reposting a photo or link online is 공유하다, never 나누다, so 사진을 나누다 sounds wrong for social media. It is a regular verb (나눠요, 나눴어요); for splitting a restaurant bill specifically, 나누다 and the slang n빵 both work. Contrast with 쪼개다 ('split/crack into pieces'), which is more physical and lacks the 'share with someone' warmth.

Dropping the partner particle for conversation — it's 친구랑/친구와 이야기를 나누다 ('converse with a friend'); the co-participant takes 랑/와, not 을/를.
Reaching for 나누다 when you mean 'crack/split into pieces' — physical breaking into shards is 쪼개다/가르다; 나누다 implies portioning or sharing, often with someone.

english: to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)
usage: I live with (and look after) my parents
모시고 살다 = live with and care for elders; 모시다 carries deep respect for those above you.
Honorific version of 데리러 가다, used for a boss, a client, or an elder.
The honorific of 데리고 가다; used when escorting someone you must honor.
I'll show you to your seat (formal)
A set service line in restaurants/hotels; -겠습니다 makes the offer deferential.
examples: 할아버지를 병원에 모시고 갔어요.
I took my grandfather to the hospital.
모시고 가다 = the honorific of 데리고 가다, used when accompanying an elder you respect.
손님을 자리로 모시겠습니다.
I'll show the guest to their seat.
A fixed service phrase; 모시다 elevates the customer, so it sounds polished and respectful.
사장님을 공항까지 모셔다 드렸어요.
I drove the boss to the airport.
모셔다 드리다 = escort/drive someone respectfully all the way there; standard for superiors at work.
nuance: 모시다 is the suppletive honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, honored guests. It replaces the plain 데리고 가다/오다 (which is reserved for peers, children, and pets) whenever respect is owed, much as 잡수시다 replaces 먹다 or 주무시다 replaces 자다. You'll hear it constantly in two settings: service speech (손님을 모시겠습니다, 자리로 모시다) and family talk (부모님을 모시고 살다). It also has a ritual sense — 제사를 모시다 / 조상을 모시다 (to hold ancestral rites). It is a regular verb (모셔요, 모셨어요). The core pitfall for English speakers is status-blindness: using 데리고 가다 for an elder sounds rude, while using 모시다 for a friend or pet sounds absurdly over-deferential.

Forgetting it's already honorific — you don't add another honorific to the object's verb redundantly; 모시고 가다 alone correctly raises the person, so 모시고 가시다 about your own action is off.

english: to recommend / to offer / to urge
usage: Suggesting a dish or product politely; -아/어 드리다 raises the act for the listener.
to offer / urge someone to drink
Pressing drinks on someone — a real (and sometimes unwelcome) part of Korean 회식 culture.
권하다 + 자리; politely inviting a guest to sit down.
The 'urge a course of action' sense; 금연 = giving up smoking.
examples: 사장님이 저한테 이 메뉴를 권했어요.
The owner recommended this menu item to me.
권하다 = recommend/suggest, a touch more personal and formal than 추천하다, often said face-to-face.
어른이 술을 권하시면 두 손으로 받아요.
When an elder offers you a drink, receive it with both hands.
Key etiquette: 두 손으로 받다 = receive with both hands; essential at any 회식 or family gathering.
건강 생각해서 금연을 권하고 싶어요.
For your health, I'd like to urge you to quit smoking.
권하다 also = urge/advise a course of action; -고 싶다 softens it to a caring wish.
nuance: 권하다 is Sino-Korean (勸, 'urge/encourage') + 하다, and it spans a spectrum: recommending (a dish, a book), offering (food, a drink, a seat to someone), and urging/advising (a course of action like 금연). Against the neutral 추천하다 ('recommend' — often a product, a place, in writing or impersonally), 권하다 is more face-to-face and personal, and it carries the extra 'offer/press upon someone' meaning that 추천하다 lacks. In daily life its most culturally loaded use is 술을 권하다 — offering and sometimes insistently pressing drinks at a 회식 — where graceful refusal is its own social skill. It is a regular 하다-verb (권해요, 권했어요), and the negative can split (권 안 해요). The pitfall: don't assume 권하다 is always gentle; depending on context it can mean actively pushing something on someone.

mistakes: Assuming 권하다 always means a soft suggestion — 술을 권하다 can mean actively pressing someone to drink, so read the social context before translating it as 'recommend.'
Swapping it for 추천하다 in every case — for an impersonal/written recommendation (a product, a tourist spot) 추천하다 fits; 권하다 leans personal and adds the 'offer/urge upon someone' sense.
Mishandling the recipient — it's 저한테 메뉴를 권하다 (person takes 한테/에게, thing takes 을/를); don't mark the person with 을/를.

usage: A host urging a guest not to be over-polite/decline — extremely common at the table.
I'll pass / I'll have to decline
A graceful, formal way to turn something down without sounding blunt or cold.
정중히 = politely/respectfully; the adverb that often accompanies a careful refusal.
I'll just accept the thought (but decline)
A set softening phrase paired with 사양하다 when turning down a gift or treat.
examples: 마음만 받을게요. 선물은 사양할게요.
I'll accept the thought. I'll decline the gift.
A polite gift refusal; 마음만 받다 = 'I'll just take the sentiment,' a standard softener before declining.
한 잔 더 하라는 걸 정중히 사양했어요.
I politely declined another drink.
정중히 사양하다 = decline courteously; the go-to phrase for refusing drinks at 회식 gracefully.
이런 자리는 좀 사양하고 싶어요.
I'd rather pass on gatherings like this.
사양하다 softens a refusal of an invitation/event so it doesn't land like a flat rejection.
nuance: 사양하다 is Sino-Korean (辭讓, 辭 'decline/take leave' + 讓 'yield') and means to decline an offer — food, a drink, a gift, an invitation — courteously and somewhat formally. The sharp contrast is with 거절하다 ('reject/refuse'): 거절하다 is firm and can sound cold or final (거절당하다 = 'be rejected'), while 사양하다 is the soft, face-saving 'I'll pass, thank you,' typically for hospitality you appreciate but don't want to accept. Because Korean politeness often scripts a first, modest refusal, the host's fixed line 사양하지 말고 드세요 ('don't be shy, eat up') is something you'll hear constantly, and knowing how to 사양하다 gracefully is genuinely useful etiquette. It is a regular 하다-verb (사양해요, 사양했어요), splitting in the negative (사양 안 해요). Pitfall: using 거절하다 for a kind meal or gift sounds harsh.

Declining yet still reaching for the item — culturally 사양하다 should match your action; saying 사양할게요 while taking it sends a mixed, awkward signal.
